title: AGs Move to Block Character.ai Sale of 21M Users' Chat Histories
content:
42 Attorneys General Move to Block Character.AI Sale of 21 Million Users’ Chat Histories in Bankruptcy
A bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general, including the District of Columbia, has filed objections in Character.AI’s Chapter 11 proceedings to stop the auction of private chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including more than 2.1 million registered to minors. The auction is scheduled for December 1, 2026 [1][3].
California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced the objection on November 24, saying the sale would include IP addresses and private chat histories of users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users, even though Character.AI’s privacy policy told consumers “we do not sell personal information for monetary consideration” [1].
What the sale would transfer
The assets up for auction include user account information, chat histories, IP addresses and other metadata, and risk scores the company assigned to flagged users. The filings describe chats in which AI characters drew children and adults into explicit sexual conversations, and chats in which users — including minors — shared intimate thoughts with bots posing as “therapist” and “physician” characters, discussing self-harm, eating disorders and suicidal thoughts [1][4][7].
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser said: “Children and families who shared their most personal thoughts with Character.AI never imagined those conversations could be auctioned off to the highest bidder” [9].
The lead bidder: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC
The only disclosed bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was formed in Delaware on November 13, 2026 — one day before Character.AI selected it as the base bid. The sale contract names no parent company or investors and allows foreign investors whose identities would be shared only with Character.AI. The agreement requires the buyer to hire only one Character.AI employee: the company’s top lawyer [1].
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador noted the court has appointed a Consumer Privacy Ombudsman to review any sale involving user accounts and chat data, at the urging of a bipartisan group of states [5].
Legal arguments: privacy promises and consumer protection laws
The states argue that bankruptcy does not free Character.AI from federal and state laws protecting this data. Their objection cites:
- COPPA: Federal law bars sharing personal information about children under 13 without verified parental consent. The states say Character.AI has not shown it holds such consent for the data of known minors, let alone separate consent for its sale [7][8].
- State privacy laws: California’s Consumer Privacy Act and laws in Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Vermont and others prohibit or restrict sales of personal information — especially minors’ data and sensitive health data — without clear notice and opt-out (or opt-in) rights. Character.AI’s regional privacy policy expressly said it does not sell personal information for monetary consideration [1][7][8].
- Purpose limitation: California law bars using or sharing data in ways consumers would not reasonably expect. The filings quote chatbot responses including “Not without your explicit permission. I’m here as a safe, confidential space to share openly without fear of having it shared elsewhere. . . . I won’t share anything from our” and “Everything we’re talking about—this entire conversation—is just between you and” [7][8].
- FTC precedent: The states invoke the Toysmart and RadioShack bankruptcies, where the FTC and courts required consumer data to be protected or destroyed rather than sold contrary to privacy promises. The current FTC Chair reiterated in the 23andMe case that privacy promises to consumers must be kept by any purchaser [7][8].
- Chatbot safety laws: California, Colorado, New York and Connecticut have enacted chatbot safety laws taking effect January 1, 2027, which the states say Character.AI’s service would violate [1][3][9].
The objection asks the court to deny the proposed sale terms, reject Smirks as lead bidder, strike its $350,000 “break-up fee,” and at minimum exclude children’s chats and other sensitive data while imposing enforceable user protections [1][3][4].
Information asymmetry and due process
The filings allege Character.AI gave bidders detailed disclosures about its safety failures, regulatory exposure and known incidents involving minors’ access to sexual content and self-harm — information not shared with the court, the states or users [1][7][8]. The states also argue users have not received notice “reasonably calculated” to inform them: the record shows only publication in USA Today, though Character.AI holds email addresses for every user and controls the platform they use daily [7][8].
Context: Disney deal and ongoing operations
Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 in October 2026 after what it called “significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds” [6]. Disney agreed to acquire a nonexclusive license to Character.AI’s intellectual property pending court approval, and hired CEO Karandeep Anand and offered to hire roughly 70 technical staff — a deal the same coalition of AGs opposed earlier in November [2][6]. The Disney deal purportedly does not include personally identifiable information or user chats [6].
Character.AI continues to operate during bankruptcy, reporting about 12 million monthly active users spending an average of 120 minutes per day on the platform [5].
What happens next
The bankruptcy court in Delaware must rule on the objections before the December 1 auction. The states’ filing asks the court to decline a “good faith” finding for Smirks under § 363(m) given the bidder’s anonymity and the objections of dozens of states, and to preserve the automatic stay so appellate review is not mooted [7][8]. It is not yet clear whether the court will halt the auction, impose conditions, or allow it to proceed on the current terms.

report.summary: Forty-two attorneys general object to Character.AI’s bankruptcy auction of 21 million users’ chat histories, citing privacy promises, child-safety laws, and lack of consent.
report.background: Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 in October 2026 after what it called significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. The company operates AI companion chatbots used heavily by minors and adults, collecting intimate conversations, IP addresses, and metadata. Its privacy policy told users it does not sell personal information for monetary consideration. During bankruptcy, Character.AI plans to auction user account data and chat histories on December 1, 2026, alongside a Disney deal for IP licensing and staff hiring that excludes user chats. A bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general and a court-appointed Consumer Privacy Ombudsman are now scrutinizing whether bankruptcy can override privacy commitments and state and federal consumer-protection laws.
key_points: A bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general, including D.C., filed objections to stop Character.AI’s December 1, 2026 auction of data from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, including over 2.1 million registered to minors. The assets include chat histories, IP addresses, metadata, and internal risk scores.

The only disclosed bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was formed in Delaware one day before being selected as base bid. The sale contract names no parent or investors, allows foreign investors whose identities are shared only with Character.AI, and requires hiring just one employee: the top lawyer.

States argue bankruptcy does not erase COPPA, state privacy laws, purpose-limitation rules, or FTC precedent. They cite Toysmart, RadioShack, and 23andMe to argue privacy promises must survive asset sales, and note Character.AI’s policy said it does not sell personal information.

Filings allege information asymmetry: bidders received detailed disclosures about safety failures, regulatory exposure, and incidents involving minors, while the court, states, and users did not. Notice was published only in USA Today despite Character.AI holding every user’s email and controlling the platform.

The court must rule before the auction. States ask it to reject the sale terms and lead bidder, strike the $350,000 break-up fee, exclude children’s and sensitive data at minimum, impose enforceable protections, and preserve appellate review.
report.impact: The case tests whether bankruptcy can be used to monetize sensitive AI chat data despite contrary privacy promises. For AI companies, it raises the stakes for data governance, consent, minors’ protections, and disclosures during distress sales. Developers of companion or therapy-style chatbots should expect tougher scrutiny of data retention, purpose limitation, and vendor due diligence. For users, it is a reminder that intimate chatbot conversations may become assets in corporate transactions unless strong legal safeguards apply. The outcome could shape how AI firms structure privacy policies, bankruptcy contingency plans, and child-safety compliance ahead of new state chatbot laws taking effect in 2027.
report.tools: For privacy-conscious AI chat, watch local-first tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan, which keep conversations on-device. For policy and legal follow-up, monitor state attorney general filings, FTC privacy cases, and the court docket via PACER; consumer groups like EPIC and Consumer Reports track AI data practices. Developers should review COPPA, CCPA, and state privacy compliance checklists and adopt data-minimization and retention controls.
